list.listitem: Maternal conditions significantly influence fetal health (see ). B
Apgar scores assess newborn requirement for resuscitation (see ); the score does not predict anoxic damage or cerebral palsy. B
Premature (<37 weeks) or low-birth-weight (<2500 g) infants may have problems with transition after birth. B
Human milk is the optimal food for newborns. B
Newborns should have a comprehensive examination within 24 hours after birth to detect problems that may necessitate transfer to a special care nursery. C
See chapter on prenatal care for information about prenatal assessment.
Key prenatal risk factors for congenital malformation include increasing maternal age and maternal diabetes.

Perinatal risk factors: Group B streptococcal infection, chlamydia or gonorrhea (neonatal infection) Rh negative (hemolysis) Serum alpha-fetoprotein high (neural tube and abdominal wall defects) or low (trisomy 21) Breech delivery (orthopedic problems such as hip dysplasia) 24-hour rupture of membranes (sepsis) Meconium-stained fluid (meconium aspiration) Forceps delivery (facial nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, and skull fracture) Vacuum extraction (scalp devitalizing, sloughing, SC bleeding)

The first ~6 hours of life is a transitional period, during which newborns must demonstrate normal respiration, cardiovascular function, and thermoregulation. Frequent monitoring is essential until the newborn is stable.

To detect anomalies or special care needs, the examination should be performed as soon as possible in premature newborns and within 24 hours in full-term newborns. A comprehensive examination should also be done at the time of discharge.
At term, an appropriate birth weight is usually 2500 to 4000 g. Birth weights should be plotted on an appropriate newborn growth curve to determine the infant's weight percentile for gestational age.

Clinical problems may be associated with abnormal birth weights. Large-for-gestational age (LGA) infants (>90%tile for gestational age) are at risk of hypoglycemia, polycythemia, and birth trauma. Small-for-gestational age (SGA) infants (<10%tile for gestational age) are at risk of hypoglycemia, hypothermia, and feeding difficulties. See chapter on intrauterine growth restriction.
Temperature: Newborns should be able to maintain an axillary temperature of 36.5°C to 37.4°C in an open crib.
Heart rate: 120 to 165/min. Bradycardia (<90/min) may occur with sleeping. Tachycardia (>180/min) may occur with crying.
Respiratory rate: 30 to 60/min.

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 eligible studies with data for 229,421 neonates, the overall sensitvity of pulse oximetry for detection of critical congenital heart defects was 76.5%; specificity was 99.9% and the false-positive rate was 0.14%.
Congenital anomalies occur in ~3% of newborns. Estimated incidence of various categories of birth defects is shown in .
Abnormal facial features () can be associated with various syndromes. See chapters on Down syndrome and fetal alcohol syndrome.
Dubowitz examination and Ballard Maturational Score provide a clinical assessment of the gestational age.
Interference with normal vision may result in permanent damage.
Newborns are nearsighted and have a fixed focus at ~8 to 12 inches. Their visual acuity is 20/300 to 20/600.

Eye examination: Slowly rotate the vertically held newborn back and forth. Newborns will “fix” on the face if the extraocular movements are normal; the eyes of a blind newborn will “wander aimlessly.” Assess the light reflex. Light should be symmetrically reflected on both pupils. Assess symmetrical red reflex.

The following eye conditions are common: Pseudostrabismus, in which the newborn looks “cross-eyed” (often because of a wide nasal bridge), but has a conjugate gaze. Delivery-induced scleral and retinal hemorrhages self-resolve by ~4 weeks. Lacrimal duct stenosis (20% of newborns) presents with eyelash crusting and adhesion; often self-resolves (70% by 3 months; 99% by 1 year). Conjunctivitis (allergic) or conjunctivitis (infectious). If <24 hours old, suspect chemical irritation from eye prophylaxis; if <1 week old, suspect Neisseria gonorrhea; if 1 to 2 weeks old, suspect Chlamydia trachomatis.

Infants with any of the following eye findings should be referred to an ophthalmologist: Leukocoria (white reflex) resulting from cataract, retinoblastoma, chorioretinitis, or retinopathy. True strabismus after 2 months. Intermittent strabismus after 3 to 4 months. Congenital glaucoma, presenting with a large cornea (>1 cm), photophobia, and tearing.
Examine the external ears for anomalies (e.g., malformed auricles and preauricular pits/tags).

Hearing loss affects 1 to 6 per 1000 newborns; failure to detect it in the first 6 months may impair language development.
Healthy full-term infants should be screened by otoacoustic emission (detects conductive hearing loss) or auditory brainstem response (ABR; detects conductive and sensorineural defects) before 1 month. Any infant admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for more than 5 days should have ABR.
Newborns are obligate nose breathers. Choanal atresia occurs in 1 per 8000 newborns; it is twice as common in females. If bilateral (in ~50%), emergent intervention is necessary.
Unilateral atresia or choanal stenosis, may present with early feeding and/or respiratory difficulties, depending on the severity of the obstruction.
Demonstrate patency of the nares (e.g., by passing a nasogastric tube).
Nasal flaring is a nonspecific sign of respiratory distress.
Evaluate for stridor.
Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor (male:female; 2:1); symptoms may not resolve until ~18 months.
Unilateral vocal cord paralysis is often well tolerated. Bilateral paralysis presents with acute respiratory distress in newborns.
Subglottic stenosis is the most common anomaly that requires tracheostomy in newborns.

Other rare causes of stridor include laryngotracheal web, cleft, fistula or cyst, tracheal compression (e.g., vascular rings, double aortic arch, anomalous innominate artery, and pulmonary artery sling) and subglottic hemangioma.
Evaluate for cleft lip and palate (1 per 700 newborns) by inspecting the lip and palate (look for bifid uvula) and by tactile palpation of the submucosal cleft.
Support the newborn head and neck (especially when picking him/her up from a supine position) because newborns have weak cervical flexor muscles.
Examine the neck for anomalies (e.g., pits, tags, cysts, and masses).
Thyroglossal duct cysts present as midline tags or fistulas.
Branchial cleft cysts present along the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Cystic hygromas (lymphangioma) present as a mass in the posterior cervical triangle.
Examine the neck for range of motion; see chapter on Torticollis.

Inspect the chest for signs of respiratory distress.
Newborns have an “abdominal breathing pattern,” as the diaphragm descends below the costal margin and the abdomen rises during inspiration. Because of their compliant chest wall and relatively large liver, lower intercostal and subcostal retractions may be present in normal newborns. Tachypnea is the most sensitive (nonspecific) sign of respiratory distress. Deep intercostal retractions and the use of accessory cervical muscles during inspiration indicate respiratory distress and increased work of breathing. Suprasternal retractions indicate upper airway obstruction.
Sneezing is common because newborns are obligate nose breathers. However, coughing is pathologic and indicates respiratory illness.

Evaluate the breath sounds.
Lack of air entry on one side may indicate pneumothorax. Grunting results from exhalation with partially closed glottic structures; this process prevents lung collapse at the end of expiration. Crackles—they may be heard immediately after birth due to fetal lung fluid. Persistent crackles, along with other signs (e.g., tachypnea, nasal flaring and grunting), may indicate transient tachypnea of the newborn resulting from retained fluid in the lungs (often seen in newborns delivered by C-section), meconium aspiration syndrome, or pneumonia. Inspiratory stridor indicates upper airway (extrathoracic) obstruction. Inspiratory plus expiratory stridor indicate severe upper airway obstruction or intrathoracic airway obstruction (e.g., vascular ring, pulmonary artery sling, extrinsic mass). Wheezing is not typically heard in newborns.

Examine for a fractured clavicle (petechiae over the midclavicular area). Palpate the clavicle for any soft tissue mass that makes the clavicle outline indistinct, or crepitus. A fractured clavicle might also be evident with an asymmetric Moro reflex (). Clavicle fracture is the most common form of birth trauma, with an incidence of 0.2% to 3.5%. A nondisplaced, greenstick fracture may be missed unless there is a high index of suspicion and low threshold for radiological imaging. Fewer than 10% of infants with clavicle fracture have Erb's palsy; the combination of these two injuries results from significant shoulder dystocia during natural delivery.
Examine for breast hypertrophy. Reassure parents that breast hypertrophy results from maternal estrogens and will regress spontaneously; lactation may occur.
Palpate the impulse at the left and right nipples; it should be stronger on the left; otherwise, “situs inversus” should be suspected.
Irregular beats often represent benign premature atrial contractions resulting from increased catecholamines.
Evaluate the heart sounds. The incidence of congenital cardiac malformations is ~1%, and only ~50% of these infants are identified on the newborn examination.
Palpate the femoral pulses. Weak femoral pulses suggest coarctation of the aorta.

The abdomen may appear distended because of swallowed air or delayed stooling. A persistently distended abdomen, especially with delayed stooling, suggests obstruction. See chapter on Hirschsprung's disease.
Many newborns have a scaphoid abdomen after passing meconium. Otherwise, a scaphoid abdomen suggests congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
Fascial defects between the rectus muscles (“diastasis recti”) present as vertical, midline bulging during crying; this normal variant resolves spontaneously.

Abdominal wall defects require surgical repair. In omphaloceles (1 of ~5000 newborns), variable amounts of abdominal contents protrude into the base of the umbilical cord; it is associated with other congenital anomalies. In gastroschisis (1 of ~10,000 newborns), variable amounts of abdominal contents herniate through the abdominal wall without a covering sac; it is associated with intestinal atresia (25%).

In “cord cutis” (a normal variant), the umbilical cord base is covered with skin and will not fall off when the upper cord separates (usually 10-14 days after birth). The cord clamp should not be placed over cord covered by skin.
A two-vessel cord is associated with spontaneous abortion, Intrauterine growth restriction , premature delivery, and renal anomalies.
See chapter on umbilical hernia.
Palpate the abdomen for masses (hydronephrosis, neuroblastoma). Liver edge can be normally felt on gentle palpation (owing to relative hyperinflation of the right lung).
Measure and plot the head circumference to detect macrocephaly (>98%) and microcephaly (<10%). An abnormal skull requires ultrasound or CT scan to evaluate hydrocephalus or intracranial anomalies.
Inspect the shape of the skull for craniosynostosis ().

Palpate the anterior and posterior fontanelles. The anterior fontanelle should be open (mean diameter, 2.1 cm), flat, and soft. It may pulsate with heartbeats, but it should not be tense, bulging (increased intracranial pressure), or sunken (dehydration). The median age for its closure is 13.8 months. The posterior fontanelle is closed in the majority of newborns. If open, it should be “fingertip sized” and close by ~2 months. Large fontanelles are seen in hypothyroidism, hydrocephalus, vitamin D deficiency, prematurity, intrauterine growth restriction, trisomy 21, and dwarfism.

Palpate the scalp. Caput succedaneum is a labor-induced subcutaneous edema/hemorrhage presenting as diffuse swelling of the scalp. It is largest at birth and self-resolves in a few days. Cephalohematoma is a labor-induced subperiosteal bleeding and does not cross suture lines. It may progress to a tense mass over 24 hours. It may calcify and take months to self-resolve. Craniotabes are benign soft areas of the skull, usually adjacent to but not contiguous with the sagittal suture. Separation of skull bones (“diastasis of the sutures”) is a normal variant if the anterior fontanelle is not bulging and there is no macrocephaly. Overriding or ridging of skull bones could be due to the labor and should self-resolve. Persistent ridging of the sutures beyond the first few week may be associated with craniosynostosis or achondroplasia.
Examine the extremities (position, range of motion).
Positional deformities of the feet and toes are common. See chapter on Abnormal gait in children.
Amniotic bands may constrict extremity blood flow, causing amputations.

Accessory (partial) digits are usually located on the ulnar side of the little (5th) finger. The digit is likely to have a bone and nerve if the nail is present; this may require surgical removal. Look for polydactyly or syndactyly of the hands and/or feet, simian creases on the palms, and clubfoot deformity (talipes equinovarus).

Examine the hips for developmental dysplasia. See chapter on Abnormal gait in children. Authors of a Cochrane review found no supporting evidence that ultrasound strategies for detecting hip dysplasia improved clinical outcomes (e.g., late detected developmental hip dysplasia and surgery) although there was a significant increase in treatment. The studies, however, were substantially underpowered. For infants with unstable hips or mildly dysplastic hips, use of delayed ultrasound and targeted splinting reduced treatment without significantly increasing the rate of late detected hip dysplasia or surgery.
Inspect the spine for deep sacral dimples, hair “tufts,” or vascular nevi (birthmarks); these findings may be associated with spinal cord abnormalities (e.g., tethered spinal cord).
Deep dimples located above the gluteal folds may be associated with a fistulous tract that communicates with the spinal canal. Further evaluation requires ultrasound of the lower spine.

Inspect the penis for length and position of urethral opening. Full-term newborns should have an unstretched penile length of greater than or equal to 2.5 cm; otherwise, they may have “microphallus.” “Ambiguous genitalia” requires endocrine consultation. Hypospadias (1 per 125 newborns) is the displacement of the urethral opening onto the (ventral) underside of the penis or base of the scrotum. Newborns with hypospadias should NOT be circumcised as the foreskin tissue may be used to repair the distal urethra. A “hooded prepuce” is incomplete development of the distal foreskin, with excess dorsal foreskin tissue and absent foreskin on the ventral surface of the penis. It may be associated with urethral anomalies. Circumcision should be done only after the location of the urethral opening is documented and the urine stream is visualized during voiding.

Inspect and palpate the scrotum and testes for hernias, hydroceles, etc. Both testes should be palpable in the scrotum or be manipulated down into the scrotum (retractile). If unable to palpate the testicle, suspect cryptorchidism (undescended testes), which is associated with underdeveloped ipsilateral hemiscrotum. Pelvic ultrasound or MRI may locate the position of a nonpalpable testis. Cryptorchidism can be associated with anomalies (e.g., neural tube defects), impaired testosterone synthesis, gonadotropin deficiency (e.g., Prader-Willi syndrome), and dysmorphic syndromes. Surgical treatment is recommended at 6 to 18 months. Long-term complications include infertility and testicular cancer.
See chapter on Inguinal hernia. A hydrocele is present when fluid has accumulated around the testicle; it can be confirmed by transillumination. Hydroceles should resolve by 6 to 12 months. Neonatal torsion accounts for ~10% of testicular torsions. The hemiscrotum is edematous and bruised and does not transilluminate. Careful examination is necessary to exclude an incarcerated inguinal hernia. Ultrasound (with Doppler flow study) and prompt surgical evaluation are necessary.
The full-term newborn's labia majora covers the labia minora and vaginal opening (vaginal introitus). The preterm newborn has underdeveloped labia majora and prominent labia minora and clitoris.

Gently spread the labia to expose the vaginal opening and hymen (an irregular circle). Maternal estrogens may cause hypertrophy of the vaginal mucosa (producing a tag, light, pink tissue protruding through the introitus) and hypertrophy of the uterine mucosa. These tags regress within a few weeks and may be associated with a whitish discharge or bleeding (pseudomenses).

A bulging, cystic, “grape-like” structure within the vaginal introitus is a hydrometrocolpos (fluid-containing cyst) resulting from imperforate hymen; incision to drain the secretions is necessary to avoid urethral obstruction.
Examine the anus for patency.
Imperforate anus (1 per 5000 newborns) requires surgical repair before initiating oral feedings.
Newborn skin has little subcutaneous tissue, which causes difficulty with thermal regulation and increased insensible water loss.
Inspect the skin for birthmarks and rashes ().
Inspect the skin for jaundice. See chapter on neonatal jaundice.
AAP raised the thresholds for treating hyperbilirubinemia in newborns born at 35 weeks' or later.

Primitive reflexes are stereotypical movements that are established at birth, and most of them disappear at 3 to 6 months (). Persistence of the primitive reflexes may indicate neurological pathology (e.g., cerebral palsy).

Erb's palsy results from stretching the nerve roots of the brachial plexus due to shoulder dystocia. The affected extremity will have the arm extended and turned inward (pronated), the wrist flexed, and the fingers able to wiggle, simulating a waiter soliciting a tip. Sensation is generally intact.

Administer monovalent hepatitis B (HepB) vaccine to all newborns prior to discharge. If the mother is hepatitis B surface Ag positive, administer hepatitis B immune globulin and HepB vaccine within 12 hours of birth.
Vitamin K at birth (IM) prevents hemorrhage, especially in breastfed newborns.
Eye drops (1% silver nitrate, 1% tetracycline, or .5% erythromycin ophthalmic ointment) at birth prevent gonococcal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum).

For healthy newborns, early skin-to-skin contact beginning at birth until after end of first breastfeeding, with placing dried, naked baby prone on mother's bare chest, covered with a warm blanket, promotes breastfeeding and better stabilization of physiological paramaters in the infant soon after birth.

Newborns should void by 24 hours and pass first meconium by 24 to 48 hours. A newborn should not be discharged until he or she has urinated and passed stool. Delayed meconium may be associated with cystic fibrosis or Hirschsprung disease, which requires appropriate work-up. See chapters on cystic fibrosis and Hirschsprung's disease.

Hypoglycemia (serum glucose <40 mg/dl) occurs in ~10% of LGA infants, ~30% of SGA infants, and 15% of premature infants. For these newborns, serum glucose should be monitored at regular intervals until stable. Symptoms of hypoglycemia include tachycardia, bradycardia, tachypnea, apnea, temperature instability, jitteriness, hypotonia, weak suck, and seizures.

Blood should typically be taken and sent for newborn screening, although specific requirements vary by location. When blood sampling is needed in term neonates, venipuncture performed by a skilled phlebotomist appears to be the method of choice for reducing pain. Oral sucrose, breastfeeding, or supplemental breast milk administration can also reduce procedural pain from short procedures such as heel lance, venipuncture and intramuscular injections.

All newborns should be screened for critical congenital heart defects after 24 hours of life, or just prior to discharge home by measuring both preductal (right hand) and postductal (either foot) saturations. A neonate passes the screen with a SaO2 ≥95% and ≤3% difference between pre- and post-ductal saturations. A neonate with a SaO2 <90% needs an immediate echocardiogram. A neonate with SaO2 between 90% and 95% or >3% difference in pre-postductal saturations should have their screen repeated in an hour. Oxygen saturation thresholds for a positive screen may differ for neonates at altitude. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 eligible studies with data for 229,421 neonates, the overall sensitivity of pulse oximetry for detection of critical congenital heart defects was 76.5%; specificity was 99.9% and the false-positive rate was 0.14%.
Data do not support the use of overgowns by attendants or visitors to the newborn nursery to prevent infection.

Umbilical cord milking for nonvigorous infants born at 35 to 42 weeks' gestation does not reduce NICU admissions. However, it is associated with a decreased need for delivery room cardiorespiratory support, lower incidence of moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, and less use of therapeutic hypothermia.
Intrapartum group B Streptococcus (GBS) antibiotic prophylaxis is not associated with an increased risk of developing asthma, eczema, food allergy, or allergic rhinitis in the first 5 years of life.

A visual assessemnt of jaundice should be obtained by 24 hours of life, or before the newborn is discharged, and newborns who are visibly jaundice should have a serum bilirubin level measured. The American Academy of Pediatrics has published bilirubin threshold at which phototherapy and exchange transfusion are recommended. See chapter on neonatal jaundice.

section.type: Indications for Transfer to Special Care Nursery
section.heading: Indications for Transfer to Special Care Nursery

list.listitem: Transfer to a higher level of care should occur if the newborn is premature (<35 weeks), has apnea, is unable to maintain temperature, is unable to feed, has persistent hypoglycemia, has unstable vital signs, has respiratory distress, or has suspected sepsis.

A Cochrane review on use of surfactant prophylaxis for preterm infants at risk of respiratory distress syndrome found that administration to infants requiring intubation along with current practice of administration of maternal steroids and routine post-delivery stabilization on continuous positive airway pressure resulted in less risk of chronic lung disease or death than routine prophylaxis.

Early administration of erythropoietin to preterm or low-birth-weight infants at less than 8 days of age results in a reduction in RBC transfusions and the volume of RBCs transfused but increases the risk of retinopathy of prematurity. As these small reductions are of limited clinical importance, the Cochrane authors of this review recommend against this practice. Likewise, late administration of erythropoietin to preterm or low-birth-weight infants 8 days or more did not significantly reduce or increase any clinically important adverse outcomes, including donor exposure.

For preterm infants, although the use of ibuprofen decreases the incidence of PDA on day three and rates of surgical ligation, there was no decrease in mortality and the PDA closed spontaneously by day three in 58% of the neonates. Because prophylactic treatment exposes infants to a drug with potential renal and gastrointestinal side effects, the Cochrane authors concluded that prophylactic ibuprofen was not recommended.
Based on three trials, Cochrane authors found lack of supporting evidence for administration of oral immunoglobulin to prevent NEC in preterm or low-birth-weight infants.
In one RCT reviewed by Cochrane authors, oral lactoferrin prophylaxis reduced the incidence of late-onset sepsis in infants weighing <1500 g (relative risk 0.34; 95% CI, 0.17-0.70).

In another RCT of 1187 infants of birthweight 501 to 2000 grams, there were no significant differences in early-onset group B streptococcal disease or neonatal mortality from use of prophylactic IM penicillin.
To reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome, infants should sleep on their backs (supine) on a firm sleep surface with no stuffed animals or loose bedding/blankets.

Parents should be educated about intracranial trauma associated with shaking (shaken baby syndrome). This form of child abuse has ~20% mortality and can result in seizures, cerebral palsy, and mental retardation.
Prior to nursery discharge, the parent should have basic infant supplies, including a properly installed rear-facing infant car seat.
Parents should be familiar with infant assessment and demonstrate competency with feeding, bathing, umbilical cord care, and circumcision (if appropriate).

Human milk is the optimal food for newborns. Mothers should be encouraged to begin nursing within the first hour and continue to nurse frequently (minimum of 15-20 minutes/feed, 10-12 times/d) until the milk supply is well established.

A Japanese randomized trial with 312 newborns found that not giving cow's milk during the first 3 days of life significantly reduces the likelihood of later food allergy (NNT = 10), including anaphylaxis (NNT = 14).
A study of infants referred because of feeding difficulty and suspected tongue-tie or lip-tie found that over 60% could be managed non-surgically.

Restricted pacifier use in healthy term breastfeeding infants did not significantly affect the prevalence or duration of exclusive and partial breastfeeding up to 4 months of age; however, there is insufficient data on the potential harms of pacifiers on infants and mothers.

Nursing mothers should avoid medications that could pass into breast milk. Active maternal tuberculosis, HIV, and human T-cell lymphotrophic viruses are contraindications to breastfeeding.
Mothers should avoid breastfeeding if they are being treated with chemotherapy or involved with illicit drug usage. Tobacco smoking and consumption of ethanol should be discouraged while breastfeeding.

Basic injury prevention includes reliable smoke detectors, hot water heaters set at less than or equal to 120°, and “child proofing” the home. Special issues should be addressed on an individual basis, such as prevention of drowning. Parents should be familiar with choking and have knowledge of, or training in, cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
Crying peaks at ~6 weeks; healthy infants may cry up to 3 h/d (often between 6 pm and midnight). See chapter on colic.
Newborns sleep for around 20 hours per day for the first 2 days and ~18 h/d by the end of first week.
Sequential allergenic food exposure (peanuts, cow's milk, wheat, and eggs) at 3 months of age decreases food allergy at 36 months.

Newborns should see their primary care provider at 4 to 5 days of age (2-3 days after nursery discharge or earlier depending on age at hospital discharge; see neonatal jaundice chapter) and then again at 2 to 4 weeks. See chapter on well child care visits for follow-up outside the newborn period.
Newborns lose 5% to 10% of the birth weight in the first few days. They should regain birth weight by ~10 days.
Children with or at high risk of cerebral palsy should receive early intervention services as soon as possible.

tr.td: Increased interpupillary distance; eyes are too far apart. Normally, the center of the eyes should align with the corners of the mouth
Decreased interpupillary distance (associated with failure of midface development)
Ears should touch a line connecting inner and outer canthi of eyes. Head molding may cause the ears to be low and rotated posteriorly
Long distance between base of nose and top margin of upper lip
Inverted “y” shaped; may indicate submucous cleft palate. It can be associated with small lower jaw (micrognathia) and upper airway obstruction (e.g., Pierre-Robin syndrome)
Skin folds covering the inner corner (“canthus”) of the eye
Distance between inner and outer canthi of the eyes
Missing a portion of the eyelid, iris (“keyhole pupil”) or retina
Each iris has a different color; associated with hearing loss
Absent iris (usually bilateral); associated with poor vision and Wilms tumor

Place the newborn in a semi-upright position and transiently allow the head to fall in the examiner's hands. The normal sequence is extending the arms outward (to the sides) with the palms facing upward and the thumbs flexed, and then coming forward and flexing (closing) the arms as if to hug something. It resolves by 4-6 mo.
Gently stroke at the corner of the mouth; the newborn will search for the finger and begin to suckle. It resolves by 2-4 mo.
Newborns will suck on a finger inserted in the mouth. It resolves by 2-4 mo.
Newborns will grasp onto a finger placed in the open palm (palmar grasp reflex; resolves by 4-6 mo) or below the toes (plantar grasp reflex; resolves by 12-15 mo).

Turn the head toward a shoulder. In response, the newborn assumes a “fencing” position, with extension of the arm and the sword hand facing the direction of the chin. The contra-lateral arm flexes at the elbow and is raised up behind the head in the “en guarde” position, as a swordsman would. It resolves by 3-4 mo.

Hold newborns in the upright position with dorsum (top surface) of the foot touching the edge of a table. There is flexion of the hip/knee, followed by extension. “Stepping” continues if the trunk is alternately tipped side-to-side. It resolves by 2-4 mo.
Premature suture fusion, usually the coronal or sagittal. The head grows in asymmetric shape, often restricting brain growth.
Asymmetric head shape from unilateral fusion of one cranial suture. Diagnosis is made on plain skull x-ray (ossification of suture).
Long, narrow head shape from fusion of the entire sagittal suture.
Wide, short head shape from bilateral fusion of the coronal sutures.
Triangular-shaped forehead due to fusion of the frontal (metopic) suture.
Tiny whitish papules on the face, resolve spontaneously.
Inclusion cysts on gum, lateral palate, or buccal/lingular mucosa.
Yellow papules over nose and cheeks, resolve spontaneously.
Fine hair covering face, trunk, extremities, resolve by 34-wk gestation.
Flat, bluish, “bruise-like” areas seen over lower spine and buttocks, fade slowly over early childhood (may mimic trauma/child abuse).
Lesions caused by occlusion of eccrine (sweat) glands; miliaria rubra indicates inflammation in eccrine glands; miliaria crystallina occurs when sweat is retained in vesicles.
Small pustular lesions on any body area; quickly rupture leaving “craters” with scaling edge that within 24 h become hyperpigmented (melanotic) macules, which fade over wk.
Seen in ~50% of term newborns, usually 1-2 d after birth; small yellow papulo-vesicular lesions on larger, erythematous macules on trunk and extremities. The lesions contain eosinophils.
Birth trauma-induced sharply demarcated, firm, plaques or nodules in the extremities, face, trunk, or buttocks. They resolve spontaneously.
A whitish, “cheese-like” substance formed from epidermal cells and secretions of fetal sebaceous glands.
Linear vesicles on the skin of the fetal presenting part or around the eyes and mouth (“Skin-Eye-Mouth Disease”).

Superficial capillary hemangiomas are pink, blanching macules common on the face (flame nevi, “Angel Kisses”) and fade after 1 y. Flame nevi on the nape of the neck (“Stork Bites”) persist as birthmarks. Deeper hemangiomas will enlarge during the 1st year to form “Strawberry hemangiomas”, which take years for involution.
Light brown birthmarks that may be isolated findings; infants with multiple spots (≥6 spots, ≥.5 cm diameter in childhood) may have neurofibromatosis.
Hypopigmented macules (white spots) may be isolated findings and pigment may appear with age. Multiple lesions may be seen with tuberous sclerosis (may develop seizures and neurologic problems).
